column1: # What one step up of each policy does to the economy (docs/ECONOMY_MODEL.md, "The policy table and the scores").
# A step down does the opposite. Resolute Desk's own table (rd/policies.tsv) gives each policy's levels, evidence
# rating, lag and its other outcomes (uninsured, poverty, crime, overdoses, border crossings, emissions, test scores);
# this table replaces its direct effects on growth, jobs, prices and gas with the channels the model works through.
# cost         $ billions a year at full effect, + adds to the deficit. "-" is Resolute Desk's figure; a list gives
#              each step's own cost from the lowest level up (0->1, 1->2, ...), where one figure would be far off.
# class        what kind of money it is, for its multiplier: purchases, infrastructure, grants, transfers, retirees,
# phase        the share of the full effect in years 1 to 5 (the money by budget year; the other channels ramp
# lag          weeks before the channels start; "-" is Resolute Desk's. The money starts after a quarter (or the lag, if
#              shorter): appropriations and tax years do not wait for a policy's effects
# immigration  net immigration, millions a year
# participation  the labour-force participation rate, points
# nairu        the natural rate of unemployment, points
# tfp_growth   productivity's growth, points a year
# capital      the user cost of capital, %
# prices       price parts' levels by the end of the phase-in, %: shelter food energy medical goods services
# oil          oil's base price, $ a barrel
# gas          gas, $ a gallon, on top of oil
# sectors      housing (% of starts), manufacturing (index points), ai (% of investment), farm, energy, tourism (index points)
# Policies not listed keep only their cost (as federal purchases, if any) and Resolute Desk's other outcomes.

column16: basis
Revenue after avoidance, with an elasticity of taxable income near 0.25 (the estimates in the literature run from 0.1 to 0.4); some pass-through business income is taxed at the top rate
The Joint Committee on Taxation's and CBO's estimates of rate changes (about $100 billion a year for 21% to 28%); a higher rate raises the user cost of capital and lowers investment
Revenue net of the lock-in that higher rates cause (realizations fall as the rate rises); a modest rise in the cost of equity
Revenue from the largest estates; small effects on saving
Revenue estimates for a 2-3% tax on fortunes over $50 million range widely because of valuation and avoidance; contested evidence
Applying the Social Security tax to earnings above the cap (the Trustees' and CBO's estimates); a small labour-supply response among high earners
The 2021 expansion's cost; families spent much of it; studies differ on whether it reduced parents' work (from none to about 1.5 million parents)
The EITC draws single mothers into work (the 1990s expansions); strong evidence
Cutting the middle brackets: CBO's multipliers for lower and middle incomes; a small rise in hours worked
Exempting tips and overtime (Treasury and JCT estimates); most of the money goes to middle incomes; some income is relabelled
Enforcement collects several dollars for each dollar spent (CBO), mostly from high earners
Caps cut discretionary spending; CBO's multipliers for federal purchases
Taxing carried interest as wages (JCT); small
Benefits for retirees, mostly spent; a slightly earlier retirement for some
A later full retirement age keeps older workers in the labour force (CBO's long-term analyses); benefits fall
Food aid is spent at once: one of the highest multipliers in CBO's range
Requirements cut caseloads; evidence on work gains is mixed (Arkansas's Medicaid rules found none)
Cash aid to poor families, spent quickly
More generous benefits lengthen job searches a little (CBO), and support spending in downturns
Disability benefits; some recipients would otherwise work (studies of denied applicants)
Income support for the elderly poor, spent at once
Food aid for mothers and babies
Free school meals free up families' food budgets
Guaranteed-income studies (the 2024 OpenResearch trial among them) find modest falls in work; weak evidence at national scale
CBO's 2019 study of a $15 minimum: about 1.3 million fewer jobs (a range from none to 3.7 million) and about a million people out of poverty; restaurant and retail prices rise
Union wage premiums raise labour costs; effects on employment are small in most studies
A higher overtime threshold raises pay for some salaried workers; small effects on hiring
Paid leave keeps new mothers attached to work (California's program)
Direct public hiring; a national guarantee would cost several hundred billion dollars a year (the Levy Institute's estimates)
Job training: results vary widely between programs
Apprenticeships raise earnings in the trades; weak evidence at scale
Banning noncompetes raises job mobility and wages (the FTC's review of the studies)
Employee status raises costs for platforms; prices of rides and deliveries rise; contested
Compliance costs, against fewer injuries

Medicare from 60 lets some people retire earlier; Medicare for everyone would cost about $3 trillion a year before new taxes (Urban Institute and RAND estimates); Medicare pays lower rates than private insurers
Medicaid's expansions covered millions; small effects on work (the Oregon experiment)
Subsidies for coverage bought on the exchanges (CBO)
Negotiated prices save Medicare money and lower drug prices; CBO expects slightly fewer new drugs over decades
A cap on what patients pay for insulin
Importing drugs from Canada and elsewhere; weak evidence of savings at scale
A public plan paying near Medicare's rates lowers premiums; how much is contested
Tax breaks for health savings accounts, mostly used by higher earners
Dental and hearing care in Medicare (CBO's estimate for the 2021 plan)
Public medical research raises private innovation, with long lags (patent studies)
Public health spending
The opioid crisis cut participation in hard-hit counties; treatment brings some people back to work
Upzoning raised building and held down rents where it happened (Minneapolis, Auckland); a federal incentive reaches some cities, not all; moderate evidence
Vouchers raise what renters can pay; with supply short, part of it goes to rents
The deduction mostly helps higher earners buy bigger homes; it is capitalized into prices
The low-income housing credit finances about 100,000 units a year; some would have been built anyway
Down-payment help raises demand faster than supply; weak evidence
Caps lower rents on covered units and discourage building (San Francisco's rent control)
Homelessness programs
Public capital raises private productivity, with returns well below the 1980s estimates (the literature since Aschauer)
Transit capital; returns depend on where it is built
High-speed rail: long lags and uncertain returns
Stricter standards raise new-car prices and lower oil demand
Chargers on the highways
Replacing lead service lines
More federal leasing adds supply over years; oil is priced worldwide, so the effect on prices is small (EIA analyses)
The 2022 credits drew factory investment and cheaper clean power; their cost depends on take-up
A $25 a ton price adds about 22 cents a gallon; with the money paid back to households, demand barely changes; strong evidence on emissions
Stricter limits raise power costs a little
New plants take years; once running they lower power costs
More exports raise production and, a little, domestic gas prices (the Energy Department's 2024 study)
Faster permits for pipelines
Transmission lines bring cheaper power to where it is used
Compliance costs, against cleaner water
Closing land to drilling and mining; small effects on supply
Electric-car rules raise new-car prices at first and lower oil demand over time
A fee on leaks from oil and gas operations
More agents and barriers reduce unlawful crossings somewhat
Tighter asylum rules lower arrivals at the border
Removals shrink the labour force, above all in farming and construction (studies of Secure Communities); contested
Legal status lets Dreamers move to better jobs and invest in skills
Half again as many green cards; CBO's analyses: a larger labour force and economy, small effects on wages
Skilled immigrants patent at high rates (studies of the H-1B lottery)
More farm guest workers hold down food prices
Mandatory checks deter some unauthorized work; farms and construction feel it; weak evidence
Refugee admissions
CBO's 2013 analysis of the Senate bill: legal status raises wages and productivity and, on net, revenue
Making data centers pay for their own power keeps others' bills down
School spending raises earnings decades later (school-finance studies); long lags
Pre-K lets parents work (Washington DC's universal program) and helps children's later earnings
Cheaper child care draws mothers into work (Quebec's program)
Grants raise college completion for low-income students
Free tuition raises enrollment; much of the money goes to students who would enroll anyway
Relief frees up borrowers' budgets; spent slowly
Vouchers and tax credits for private schools; contested effects on learning
Teacher pay
University research raises productivity with long lags
Required testing slows some deployments; weak evidence either way
One federal rule instead of fifty state rules
Chip-plant subsidies under the 2022 law drew large investments; years to build
Tougher enforcement lowers markups; contested effects on innovation
Rural broadband
Higher capital requirements raise the cost of credit a little and make crises rarer (the Basel studies)
Limits on bank fees
NASA's budget
Defense purchases; CBO's multipliers for federal purchases
Aid is mostly spent abroad, so it adds little to demand at home
Veterans' care
Stricter domestic-content rules raise what the government pays and shift some work home
Stricter controls cost chip makers sales abroad
Missile defense
The nuclear arsenal
Trade adjustment assistance: retraining and income support
Duty-free small parcels hold down prices for cheap imported goods
Farm subsidies, mostly to larger farms
Shipbuilding and munitions plants
